Stocks mostly slid Thursday on renewed concerns around spending by artificial intelligence companies, while oil prices jumped amid rising geopolitical tensions.
The Nasdaq Composite pulled back 2.6% to 26,008.86, while the S&P 500 shed 1.21% to close at 7,663.43. The tech-heavy index suffered its worst session since June, while the S&P 500 posted its worst daily performance since July. The Dow Jones Industrial Average inched up 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to end at 52,867.98.
Meta Platforms slipped about 7%, even as it exceeded revenue expectations and offered upbeat guidance. Technology more broadly was under pressure as well as ongoing concerns about artificial intelligence spending persisted. Advanced Micro Devices fell more than 8%, while Micron Technology and Nvidia dropped 6% and 4%, respectively.
Neocloud leader CoreWeave , whose bond yields and credit default swaps remained elevated , declined 10% as well. The move comes as Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang told CNBC Thursday that demand for neoclouds is " off the charts ." However, he added that capital is scarce and impeding growth.
Huang's commentary about a scarcity of capital is "spooking markets and reigniting the concerns around the capital markets on the credit side being full from a risk appetite standpoint," said Wells Fargo traders in a note. They also said Meta's comments about the large amount of AI funding needed caused the shares to roll over and weighed on the overall market.
JPMorgan traders noted that Wednesday's bullish "tone reversed overnight" because Meta shares rolled over in the premarket and chatter increased "over renewed Iran kinetic-risk post US mid-term election."
Additionally, "underlying price actions and feedback from our trading desk also suggested the still fragile narrative around AI financing concerns and the lack of conviction/re-grossing from the recent tech reversal," they said in a note to clients.
Oil prices, meanwhile, jumped after The New York Times reported, citing sources, that the U.S. and Israel have plans for renewed strikes against Iran following next month's midterm U.S. elections. President Donald Trump also told reporters late Wednesday that Washington is not negotiating with Tehran and that something will happen "fairly soon."
International benchmark Brent crude futures rose 4% to settle at $113.17 per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude futures advanced 2.39% to $99.47 per barrel.
Investors also turned to U.S. Treasurys in their search for a safe haven. The benchmark 10-year Treasury note yield dropped more than 17 basis points to 4.972%, falling to its lowest level in almost a month . The 2-year note yield also shed more than 16 basis points to 4.659%.
The S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite saw sizable declines on Thursday.
The broad market index moved down 1.21% to 7,663.43, while the tech-heavy index decreased 2.6% to 26,008.86.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average, however, traded just above the flatline, rising 11.89 points, or 0.02%, to 52,867.98.
Shares of power and energy companies tied to the AI boom plunged Thursday as investors grew increasingly concerned about the soaring costs of data center expansion.
Two major energy equipment players, GE Vernova and Bloom Energy , led the declines, with each falling more than 11%. As investors sold their AI infrastructure stocks, Vistra also shed over 10%, while Quanta Services dropped more than 8%. Talen Energy and Eaton declined 8.3% and nearly 7%, respectively.
The selloff came as Meta's latest earnings report reignited concerns over AI infrastructure spending. The tech giant raised its capital expenditure forecast, highlighting the enormous investment required to support its AI ambitions and raising questions about how quickly those investments will generate returns.
Nuclear energy stocks were also caught in the downturn, with Oklo falling more than 4% and NuScale Power declining over 3%. The broad retreat shows a deeper, growing investor unease over whether the pace of AI infrastructure investment is sustainable.
Oil prices spiked Thursday as investors fear escalation in the Middle East with the U.S. reportedly planning to resume strikes against Iran.
Brent crude futures gained 4% to close at $113.17 per barrel, the highest level for the international benchmark since May 4. U.S. West Texas Intermediate gained 2.4% to settle at $99.47.

Moderna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its closely watched cancer vaccine developed with Merck .
The stock fell even though the full data, released later Thursday following the leak, appeared positive relative to Wall Street expectations. "Engagement failed to respond to rising investment, and last week's content leadership changes convince us that solutions require patience & lower incremental margins. Attention economy competition is rampant. Consensus estimates look fair. Downgrade to Peer Perform," Wolfe's analyst Peter Supino said.

The analyst pointed to growing competition from YouTube and rival streaming platforms, adding  that higher programming costs may weigh on Netflix's future profit margins. articles.title_orig: China: Panic as 7.0-magnitude earthquake rocks Tibet
articles.title_zh: China: Panic as 7.0-magnitude earthquake rocks Tibet
articles.content_orig:
By PERKIN AMALARAJ, FOREIGN NEWS REPORTER
Published: 11:01 EDT, 22 October 2026 | Updated: 12:08 EDT, 22 October 2026
A massive earthquake of magnitude 7 struck Tibet today, just two months after devastating Nepal glacier flood.
China 's Earthquake Networks Centre (CENC) said the quake struck at around 10.30pm local time (2.30pm UK time).
Data indicated the epicentre was in a high-altitude county in Nagqu, northern Tibet, at a depth of 6.21 miles.
It struck around 250 miles away from the Tibetan capital of Lhasa. CENC said the tremor was felt in the local area.
It is not whether anyone has been injured or killed following the latest earthquake.
Just last year, a 7.1-magnitude earthquake struck Tibet's Tingri County. Up to 400 people were killed in the region alone, while a further 13 were killed in Nepal.
Damage was seen in northern India , while the tremors were felt across south Asia .
Tibet is among the most earthquake-prone regions in the world. It sits on top of both the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates.
A woman walks past damaged houses in the aftermath of flash floods at Trishuli in Nepal's Nuwakot district on September 11, 2026
Though their continual collisions created the Himalayan mountain range, they also create countless earthquakes.
As a result, the country sits on top of many major fault lines, including the Altyn Tagh Fault and the Xianshuihe Fault System.
In 2010, a magnitude 7.1 tremor struck Yushu, around 280 km away in neighbouring Qinghai province, killing at least 2,698 people and leaving nearly 300 people missing.
The latest quake comes just a few months after Tibet and neighbouring Nepal suffered powerful and devastating floods .
Following a series of flash floods and debris flows, at least 43 people died and 519 people went missing in Tibet.
Nepal saw at least 1,455 people die and 5,285 people go missing.
The UN's climate loss and damage fund moved Thursday to provide $20million (£15million) in aid sought by flood-stricken Nepal, the first time it has set aside money for any country, in a key test of the body's credibility.
In the first extraordinary meeting since its launch in 2022, the fund's board agreed to earmark the modest sum for the Himalayan country.
'Hearing no objections, the decision is so adopted,' Camila Minerva Rodriguez Tavarez, co-chair of the board, said following a virtual meeting.
The decision does not, however, mean that Nepal will immediately receive the funding, which amounts to less than 0.5 percent of the government's $4.78billion (£3.57billion) estimate for reconstruction.
Twenty million dollars is the maximum amount countries can request in a single application.
Nepal will first have to present a proposal, and that proposal will have to be approved by the fund's board. There is no firm timeline for the process.
The creation of the 'Fund for responding to Loss and Damage' was hard-won by developing countries, and greeted with standing ovations, at the UN climate conferences of 2022 and 2023 (COP27 and COP28).
But since it became operational, critics have faulted both the meager pledges from governments - $822million (£614million) to date - and a disbursement cycle disconnected from climate disasters.
No money has been disbursed so far.

Illustration: Sarah Grillo/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
Major U.S. banks are detecting unauthorized third-party AI agents operating inside customer accounts, with some agents attempting to take actions that appear to be independent of user instructions, sources tell Axios.
Why it matters: AI agents are becoming a nightmare for America's banks, making their way into banking systems faster than financial institutions can respond.
Driving the news: Banks including Morgan Stanley, Bank of America, JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and others are racing to contain agent risks. Some are aware of unauthorized access, people familiar with the issue said.
What they're saying: Bank executives described the situation as horrifying, with one official saying the industry has grave concerns about agents gaining access to customer accounts and taking steps that could impact user finances.
State of play: The concerns are at the root of the decision by several banks to restrict third-party AI agent access, the people said.
Zoom out: Most banks have authorized or are moving in the direction of allowing read-only access , which should allow agents to see customer financial information without taking action.
Reality check: Several industry and bank executives told Axios they recognize the need to find a middle-ground with AI agents.
Threat level: Many banks are broadly not able to parse whether agent account activity is user-directed, sources said.
What we're watching: On one hand, banks are best positioned to respond to the threats and opportunities of AI given their cash on hand and experience as critical infrastructure.
The bottom line: The rapid pace of AI advancement is becoming a security nightmare for America's financial institutions.

Large demonstrations descended into disorder in Paris and across France on Saturday
Paris is extending a partial curfew restricting movement in parts of the city until Monday, as Marseille and Lyon impose a total ban on protests this weekend.
The Louvre, Orsay and Picasso museums in the French capital will also be closed on Saturday as more demonstrations are expected.
France is still reeling from major disorder at the weekend, when large protests against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.
In other parts of the country where protests have not been banned completely, only authorised union demonstrations will be allowed on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron said.
Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.
France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.
GÃ©rald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.
Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.
Police in Paris said its curfew in Place de la RÃ©publique, where protesters gathered last weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area will be extended until Monday.
Movement will be prohibited in both areas from 23:00 local time (21:00 GMT) until 06:00 the following morning, the prefecture for the capital city said, adding that it had been ordered by Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez and Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu.
Public transport Marseille will be suspended on Saturday to try to prevent a repeat of the riots in the city.
The city saw some of the worst violence last weekend and damage to more than 500 businesses.
The prefecture for the RhÃ´ne region - which covers Marseille - said a curfew for minors would be extended to the entire population overnight on Saturday 24 October, from 23:00 until 05:00 (21:00 - 03:00 GMT).
Similar announcements have been made in Nice in the south, Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.
Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.
"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced.
"When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."
He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".
Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.
The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.
Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.
Prime Minister SÃ©bastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.
Unrest spread across several French cities last weekend, including the capital Paris
Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests .
Marches were largely peaceful and took place in several major French cities, including Paris, backed by unions, gilets jaunes and student groups. But they were marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction.
Lyon's tourism office was set on fire by demonstrators during last weekend's protests.
In the city of Limoges, the clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.
A second suspect aged 66 was arrested on Thursday, after a man in his 30s was detained on suspicion of the attempted murder of police officers who were in the city hall when the fire started.
The iconic Place de la RÃ©publique was vandalised in the capital, Paris, when groups of rioters took over parts of the city, wreaking havoc.
The unrest has come as Macron enters the final months of his presidency, with elections scheduled for 18 April and 1 May next year.

articles.title_orig: Moderna’s Stock Plummets After Cancer-Vaccine Data Shared on Social Media
articles.title_zh: Moderna’s Stock Plummets After Cancer-Vaccine Data Shared on Social Media
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Two months ago, Moderna's ( MRNA ) melanoma vaccine handed the stock its best day ever. Now leaked results from the same trial have handed it its biggest intraday drop on record.
The stock fell as much as 26% before closing down more than 17%. That's still its worst day since Aug. 20, the session right after its best day.
More than $17 billion in market value has vanished as details from the late-stage trial circulated ahead of their official debut . Merck ( MRK ), Moderna's partner on the vaccine, confirmed the results came out early. The full data is set for release Saturday at Europe's biggest cancer conference, in Madrid.
The leaked numbers are still good. The personalized vaccine, paired with Merck's blockbuster Keytruda, reportedly cut the risk of the cancer returning or death by 42%. An earlier, smaller trial showed 49%, though it used different patients, so it isn't a direct comparison. The bigger issue is how much the stock had already run, nearly quadrupling from mid-August to Wednesday.
Merck fell nearly 4% at its low before paring more than half the drop. The vaccine is central to Moderna's story, but it's just an add-on for Merck.
The rest of healthcare is rallied. Eli Lilly ( LLY ) is added more than $33 billion in market value, about twice what Moderna lost. Johnson & Johnson ( JNJ ) and Pfizer ( PFE ) rose, too.
The iShares Biotechnology ETF ( IBB ) and SPDR S&P Biotech ETF ( XBI ) were only modestly lower, roughly in step with the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ).
On Aug. 19, Moderna rocketed 177% to close at $174.38 after the company said the trial met its goals. It kept climbing from there, and on Wednesday, it posted its highest close since December 2021.
Thursday's low came within 4% of that August close before buyers stepped in. A sustained break below $174 would put $116 in focus. That's where trading opened on the record day.
Watch Saturday's full data, especially how lower-risk patients fared.

Biotech research aimed at lifesaving cures. Beijing is turning all of them into instruments of military power. U.S. national security policy must catch up.
Cellular modules, advanced robotics , and biotechnology serve very different purposes, but they expose the same problem. articles.content_orig:

BAB EL-MANDEB, Yemen — To visit Bab el-Mandeb is to understand that old adage about looks being deceiving. For this humble fishing village in Yemen, a tumbledown grouping of barely-there huts nestled between the water and an imposing mountain range, stands sentinel over one of the world’s most vital waterways.
The village shares its name with the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, the narrow passageway connecting the Red Sea with the Arabian Sea that’s become another flash point in the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
“You hear so much about Bab el-Mandeb, you’d think we would be like New York, with skyscrapers and money,” said Saleh, a 58-year-old resident who, like all people interviewed here, refused to give their full name to avoid reprisals.
“So many ships pass near here. If the Yemeni government knew how to invest in it, we would be rich. We should be bringing in billions of dollars. Instead, look around you,” he said, pausing as his gaze took in the sorry-looking boats haphazardly laid on the beach.
Saleh was interviewed in January, when Bab el-Mandeb was thrust into the power struggle between Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates, the friendly-but-occasionally-fractious backers of Yemen’s internationally recognized government.
That war of wills ended with the Emirates ceding control of Bab el-Mandeb — along with the nearby island of Perim, where the Emirates had built a drone airbase — to Saudi Arabia.
But this month, control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait switched once more, when the Houthis, Yemeni rebels backed by Iran, ousted government forces from the waterway in a blitzkrieg in which they seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast .
The move grants the Houthis a valuable foothold in controlling the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a ribbon of Red Sea — known as the “Gate of Tears” for the dangers involving its navigation — between Yemen’s coast and Djibouti and Eritrea.
About 7% of global energy supplies and around 12% to 15% of all global shipping transit the strait. And in taking Perim Island , which lies in the middle the Red Sea at the strait’s narrowest point (a mere 12½ miles), the Houthis could harass ships with ease.
“We don’t need a drone or a missile,” one Houthi commander bragged in a social media video posted from the island. Instead, he added, all they had to do was place a few artillery units on Perim’s coast and they would be able to strike any ship crossing the strait.
The impact of any movement disruption through Bab el-Mandeb wouldn’t be limited to already skittish energy markets: To enter the Suez Canal’s southern entrance, ships must first transit through Bab el-Mandeb, meaning any trouble in the passageway would force freighters to circumnavigate the African continent — adding anywhere from 12 to 21 days to voyages and spiking fuel costs.
A shipping disaster in 2021 shows how blocking the strait — and thus severing a link to the Mediterranean Sea — could harm global commerce. A container ship in the Suez Canal ran aground and blocked the waterway for six days, delaying the delivery of billions of dollars of goods.
More recently, the Houthis sealed off the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in 2023 to coerce Israel into stopping its campaign in Gaza; that pushed the U.S. to attack the Houthis, before the Trump administration agreed to a ceasefire of its own with the group.
These days, the Houthi advance comes at a particularly fraught moment, one in which Bab el-Mandeb has taken on outsize importance. With the Israeli-U.S. war on Iran  prompting Tehran to seal the Strait of Hormuz —  cutting off the world’s most important energy passageway — Persian Gulf oil powerhouses have been forced to divert crude exports to alternatives, including Bab el-Mandeb.
That’s especially true for Saudi Arabia, which turned to its East-West pipeline and exports through the Red Sea to sidestep the trouble in Hormuz. But it’s also the most vulnerable to the Houthi threat.
The Houthis have a long-running animus against the Saudis, which began in 2015, months after the Houthis overran the Yemeni capital of Sanaa in 2014. Saudi Arabia, spooked about the notion of an Iranian ally on its border, led a coalition — with U.S. backing — to dislodge them. It started a blockade and a devastating air campaign that persisted until a 2022 truce.
But in July, the ceasefire broke after the Houthis accused the Saudis of striking Sanaa‘s airport in what appeared to be an attempt to stop Iranian flights from landing there. The Houthis began attacking Saudi Arabian oil infrastructure and declared a naval blockade against the kingdom.
The rebels’ land grab this month stunned Saudi Arabia, which failed to launch airstrikes and stanch the rout of its allied forces from the coast. Saudi leaders reportedly reached out to President Trump to push the rebels back, but he appears disinclined to help.
Still, on Wednesday, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, “We have a very strong defense agreement with Saudi Arabia, and we will live up to our commitments in that agreement.” He did not elaborate on what U.S. support that would entail.
On Thursday, Saudi Arabia said its defenses intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by the Houthis towards Taif, a manufacturing center, and Yanbu, a port on the Red Sea. It responded with hundreds of strikes on the Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen.
For their part, the Houthis insist they have no plans to attack shipping on the Red Sea and that their blockade applies only to Saudi Arabia — a move calculated to prevent the rise of an international effort to dislodge them.
“They don’t want to attract international military operations,” said Mohammad al-Basha, founder of the Basha Report, a U.S.-based risk advisory.
“They realize that when you do things in the Red Sea, you create panic in the world.”
But leaders in the internationally recognized Yemeni government say the Houthis are not to be trusted.
“The Houthi militias’ use of the safety of navigation as a tool for blackmail threatens not only Yemen. It is taking hostage the entire global economy,” Yemeni Vice President Abdullah Abdulkader al Alimi-Bawzer said at the United Nations General Assembly on Thursday.
He added that protecting the Bab el-Mandeb Strait is the responsibility of “every economy that depends on secure supply chains, energy security and freedom of navigation.”

The company saw strong growth in facilities management and critical infrastructure services, executives said Thursday, but project management growth dipped as corporations cut real estate spending.
CBRE’s revenue grew 13% year over year to $11.5 billion, the company reported . On a net revenue basis, its project management business grew 11%, driven in part by growth in infrastructure projects. That segment “is a very large part of our project management business [and] more than [offsets] the slowdown in real estate,” Giamartino said.
CBRE’s critical infrastructure services business — which includes network infrastructure, mechanical, engineering and plumbing projects and facilities management for data centers — is expected to generate nearly $4.5 billion of revenue in 2027, according to Sulentic.
Its acquisition of a global IT infrastructure company, Onnec Group Limited, will help drive the growth, said Sulentic, adding that even if data center growth in the U.S. eases, growth is expected to increase in other countries.
“Our acquisition of Onnec, which we announced today, fits within this line of business,” Sulentic said.
The $610 million cash deal provides CBRE with technical capabilities related to design, deployment and maintenance of network, fiber and data center infrastructure, a specialty area that’s critical to data centers, per a release Tuesday .
If the business achieves the entirety of the deal’s earn-outs, the deal will end up costing CBRE a little over $1 billion, which the firm is using as an incentive to continue to generate strong growth, Giamartino said.
The firm expects to close the acquisition by the end of the year, said Giamartino, noting that if the acquisition were included, the firm’s critical infrastructure services business would have generated approximately $3 billion in revenue over the past 12 months.
Although the company’s enterprise facilities management posted solid growth, it’s facing pressure from a handful of problematic accounts. “That’s happened from time to time over the years,” Sulentic said. “The market gets frothy, it gets more and more competitive and you … end up with some broker hires or outsourcing or enterprise accounts that don’t have the characteristics you would want.”
CBRE’s project management revenue slowed, up 3% year over year, as corporate clients acted more conservatively due to uncertainty in the economy, Sulentic said.
“We do a lot of work for big tech clients that have moved their spending away from … traditional legacy real estate-type investment into infrastructure, critical infrastructure, data centers,” he said. “I think you’re seeing some of that.” The firm also saw “a little bit of concentration slowdown in healthcare,” he said.
“What we really need is for rates to stabilize,” Giamartino said. “The volatility and the uncertainty is what’s driving a pause or a hold or even delaying deals to 2027. We expect that stability to come in the back half of next year….  Of course, if that doesn’t come or things change, the results will be different.”
In the U.S., leasing revenue rose 4%, supported by industrial, which was up 16%,  while office leasing dipped 2%, Giamartino said.
This dip, which contrasts with a broader office recovery occurring in the market, is the result of some big deals that slipped into Q4, “which is in part why we have confidence that we’ll see double-digit growth in leasing in Q4.,” she said.
Despite the cautious economic outlook, Sulentic believes that even if things slow down in the U.S. — either because of the interest rate or political environment — CBRE believes growth will accelerate globally, especially in the data center sector.
“Onnec puts us in a great position to take care of that,” Sulentic said. Even if data center growth slows in the U.S., there should be plenty of business involving existing facilities. “We think that in data centers, you’re going to see potentially some pressure on the amount of new build,” he said. “And then what’s happening, and we’re already seeing it, is a lot of refit of existing data centers.”
Outside of its critical infrastructure business, CBRE’s infrastructure services work consists of overseeing the construction of transportation and energy assets along with data centers within project management, as well as sales, leasing and financing for data centers and advisory services. When taking this work into account, CBRE expects its total infrastructure services revenue to spike 40% from this year to $7 billion in 2027, Sulentic said.

Moderna shares dropped as much as 25% on Thursday following the leak of partial data on its closely watched cancer vaccine developed with Merck .
The stock fell even though the full data, released later Thursday following the leak, appeared positive relative to Wall Street expectations. The personalized vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, paired with Merck's immunotherapy Keytruda reduced the risk of recurrence or death in certain melanoma patients by 42% compared with Keytruda alone.
The data also showed the shot along with Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 38%, compared with just the immunotherapy.
The detailed phase 3 trial results were set to be presented at the European Society for Medical Oncology conference this weekend.
Investors see the targeted vaccine as a possible breakthrough treatment, with the potential to be used in other forms of cancer in the future. It could also offer Moderna a critical additional commercial product in its pipeline, following vaccines for Covid-19, the flu and respiratory syncytial virus.
The high expectations for the product have sent Moderna shares soaring this year. The stock has spiked more than 530% year-to-date as of Thursday afternoon.
Shares of Merck, a much larger drugmaker, fell by about 1% on Thursday. The company's stock has climbed nearly 41% this year.
Since the vaccine is personalized, the complicated manufacturing process can take six weeks. But Merck CEO Robert Davis told CNBC last week that the company believes it can shorten that timeline in the future, potentially allowing the shot to reach more patients more quickly.

articles.title_orig: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
articles.title_zh: Zuckerberg wins Meta deal to help him foot bill for possible California billionaire tax
articles.content_orig:
Meta has agreed to a new deal with chief executive Mark Zuckerberg to prevent him from leaving California over a proposed state tax on billionaires.
The agreement gives Zuckerberg, whose wealth is estimated to exceed $200bn (£149bn), even more shares in Meta to make up for the fraction of his fortune he may lose if the tax wins voter approval in November.
The measure would impose a one-time 5% tax on residents with a net worth of more than $1bn. It would likely see the Facebook co-founder pay around $10bn in additional state taxes.
He secured the deal with a special committee of Meta after "robust" and "at several points, contentious" negotiations, according to a Wednesday financial disclosure.
California is home to most of the US's technology giants and there are around 225 billionaires who reside in the state, according to the Americans for Tax Fairness campaign group.
The wealth of such people, including Zuckerberg, has ballooned in recent years. Meanwhile, his estimated effective tax rate in California was less than 1% each year.
Nevertheless, Zuckerberg told Meta's board last month that he was thinking of moving his primary residence out of California, and even selling his property in the state. His main homes in Californa are in Palo Alto and Lake Tahoe.
Such a move "would be public and inevitably noted and commented upon by company employees", Zuckerberg told the board.
It would also "raise questions for management of the company going forward", he claimed.
In response, Meta decided to create more shares of stock in the company in order to give Zuckerberg a way to essentially make up any wealth he may lose through the tax proposal.
Through what's known as a stock split announced by the company on Wednesday , Meta created an entirely new type of stock and gave one new share to each existing shareholder. Zuckerberg is one of the company's largest shareholders and famously controls the company through the design of his holdings.
Through the deal, he will receive more stock, more often, and also be able to sell it on a quarterly basis, according to the company's financial filing. The shares will not change his level control over Meta, but they will allow him to cash in more easily on the company's value.
The deal appears to be effective even if the one-time tax in California does not pass, and will go on for eight years - as long as Zuckerberg remains a resident of California.
Meta called the deal with Zuckerberg its "Founder Alignment Agreement," saying it was "critically important" to keep him leading the company from California given the "dramatic and unprecedented transformation taking place in the tech industry and global economy related to artificial intelligence."
The company alluded to problems the company experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic, when Zuckerberg began working outside of the office and mostly from his large compound in Kauai, Hawaii.
After a surge in hiring at Meta during the pandemic, a whistleblower scandal that led to renewed focus on child safety, and a refocus within the company to building out the "metaverse," which included renaming the company Meta from Facebook, the company began mass layoffs and restructuring.
Layoffs have continued into this year. The company's headcount is down 15% from a year ago, meaning it has shed at least 10,000 workers.
Today, the company has moved away from the "metaverse," or virtual platforms, and is more focused on artificial intelligence products and related tools.
With Zuckerberg leading the company's efforts to catch up in the AI race, Meta's board said it sees a future of "tremendous market opportunity" for the company.
Major tech companies are set to spend an estimated $1 trillion this year alone developing AI and the costly infrastructure around it, like data centres .
Meta said on Wednesday it planned to spend as much as $145bn this year on AI projects. The company has increased the amount it expects to spend on AI each financial quarter so far this year.
It is spending so much on the technology that it posted negative cash flow for the first time since the company went public 14 years ago. Cash flow represents the money a company retains after paying for operations and investments, meaning Meta is now spending more money than it is bringing in.
And the company intends to spend even more in the year ahead. Susan Li, Meta's chief financial officer, said on Wednesday that another benefit of the stock split would be to give the company more ways to finance future spending on AI work.
The degree of the company's spending on AI, without an clear new revenue stream coming from it, appeared to spook investors on Thursday.
Meta's shares fell more than 7%, wiping more than $100bn off of the company's market capitalisation, a key metric used worldwide to measure the value of a publicly-traded company.

Last week in a separate incident on I-80, a driver said he was asleep and using FSD when his Tesla plowed into a police car that was stopped at the scene of an accident. After that incident, CHP warned drivers that “Despite its name, full self-driving is not fully autonomous. A Los Angeles-based United Airlines pilot has sparked security fears for openly expressing sympathies for Iran and an allied terrorist organization.
Israel’s Transportation Ministry notified United Airlines on Wednesday that pilot Sina Amjadian is barred from entry, the Jerusalem Post reported , for sharing controversial posts on his social media.
Amjadian’s bio on Instagram describes himself as “Persian made” and based out of Los Angeles International Airport. It has a heart icon next to IKA, the abbreviation for Tehran’s international airport.
The biggest news, opinion and culture shaping California right now.
He shared images on social media featuring Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, alongside Islamic Republic flags, while criticizing Israeli military strikes in Iran.
Two posts specifically seemed to have struck a nerve with Israel. In one video, he reportedly kissed and saluted the Iranian regime’s emblem.
In a second piece of content, he allegedly expressed support for the Revolutionary Guards and Hezbollah, which is considered a terrorist organization by the US.
“The pilot’s details were forwarded to the relevant aviation security authority […] to ensure that he would not be permitted to enter Israel as a member of an aircraft crew,” an Israeli Transport Ministry spokesperson said to The Travel .​​
Information was forwarded to Israeli intelligence and defense agencies, which reviewed the findings and then made the recommendation to bar him from entry.
The California Post reached out to both United Airlines and Amjadian for comment.
The airline told the California Post that Amjadian is not currently flying for the company and has been on leave since 2024.
It’s not immediately clear if he is back in the cockpit, though he was still posting flight videos in recent days on his Instagram and his LinkedIn shows him still with United since November 2022.
Before United, he was a pilot with flydubai, and according to the Jerusalem Post, he is likely currently staying in Dubai.
It was also determined that Amjadian does not operate international routes but mainly flies domestic within the US and Canada.
Israel’s action comes in light of the recent attempted terrorist attack by a co-pilot on a flydubai plane bound for Israel.
The co-pilot started working for flydubai just months before he allegedly stabbed the main pilot in a feared terrorist hijacking on a September flight to Tel Aviv, leaving it plunging 18,000 feet.
Since then, the country has been stepping up its scrutiny. United Airlines released an internal memo to employees warning that crew members of 29 nationalities, such as from countries like Oman and Iraq, are prohibited from working on all routes to Israel.

Tech giant Oracle has added a lot of debt lately, which is drawing questions from Wall Street investors. Our colleagues Rick Mulvey and Adrian Ma at The Indicator explain how Oracle's fortunes and the AI boom connect to the wider economy.
ADRIAN MA, BYLINE: Oracle is one of those companies that you've probably heard of but may not deal with directly. It's a multinational tech giant that sells enterprise software and computing power.
RICKY MULVEY, BYLINE: Yeah. The vast majority of big companies use its databases and software.
MA: And about a decade ago, credit analysts viewed Oracle bonds as a safe investment.
MATT SHERIDAN: They were a high-margin software company. Now they're a capital-intensive data center buildout? This was a huge shift.
MA: Matt Sheridan is a senior lecturer in the finance department at...
SHERIDAN: The Ohio State University.
MULVEY: Matt analyzed credit before working as a professor too.
SHERIDAN: The biggest issue with Oracle is that load has nearly doubled in the last two years. They're sitting at 169 billion in total debt.
MA: Oracle went into the AI boom in a weaker financial spot than other tech giants.
MULVEY: Larry Ellison is the co-founder, executive chairman at Oracle. He thinks that training AI models is a huge business opportunity.
MA: So why aren't Oracle investors happy?
MULVEY: One reason is the sheer size of the debt. It's turned Oracle from a business that generates cash into one that burns money.
MA: Another is that the path back to profitability may take some time. Building data centers takes a second.
MULVEY: Oracle is relying on OpenAI a lot. Sam Altman and the folks at OpenAI promised Oracle they would pay about $300 billion over the next five or so years. Oracle's data centers help power ChatGPT.
MA: And OpenAI's financials come with a lot of open questions, mostly because you probably can't see them.
MULVEY: And Matt says if OpenAI's financials were out in the open, its value would also be based on its actual numbers.
SHERIDAN: So if you can't really trust that OpenAI's revenues are going to be growing at parabolic speed, that trickles into Oracle.
MA: Oracle and OpenAI are not just in a customer-seller relationship. This bit has more implications for the wider economy.
MULVEY: OpenAI pays Oracle to use its cloud infrastructure and says it'll pay a lot more in the coming years. So Oracle buys chips from Nvidia to build this cloud even more. And then Nvidia invests money into OpenAI so that OpenAI can buy computing space from Oracle, which, remember, is buying those Nvidia chips.
MA: I'm just picturing a circle. And according to credit investors, Oracle is a weak link in this circular economy.
MULVEY: Oracle has already signaled that it may run into trouble paying back its loans on time. This notice created some alarming headlines, but Matt says it actually could benefit Oracle. It allows the company to delay payments, though it's still on the hook for the full amount.
MA: Still, Oracle's credit investors are pricing in more risk. S&P, the big credit rating agency - they downgraded Oracle's credit in July. Now Oracle is barely above junk status. Matt says these circular deals and heavy amounts of debt could lead to real problems for the economy as a whole.
SHERIDAN: And that makes me concerned that if this is a bubble, it's going to be more like a Lehman Brothers-type event. And they're all becoming very interconnected.
MA: For now, the wheel is still turning.

articles.title_orig: Elon Musk says Tesla will sell 5 million cars by 2030 — math says otherwise
articles.title_zh: Elon Musk says Tesla will sell 5 million cars by 2030 — math says otherwise
articles.content_orig:
Musk is targeting 5 million annual vehicle deliveries by 2030, but after back-to-back years of falling sales, banking on unproven robotaxis instead of an affordable EV makes that goal look practically impossible.
Musk is targeting 5 million annual vehicle deliveries by 2030, but after back-to-back years of falling sales, banking on unproven robotaxis instead of an affordable EV makes that goal look practically impossible.
On Tesla’s earnings call Wednesday, Elon Musk made one of his patented pie-in-the-sky predictions that typically sends his fans into paroxysms of ecstasy: 5 million vehicle deliveries by 2030.
“We were aiming for 5 million vehicles a year by approximately 2030,” he said. “And I think we’ve got a good shot of achieving that goal.”
You’d be forgiven for missing the statement amid the veritable firehose of Musk superlatives — the company’s Terafab chip factory “will be the most valuable building in the world” with “an economic value that’s going to be placed in the top 20 countries” and “Tesla will end up being a majority of all passenger miles on Earth in any country where it is allowed to operate freely” — but nevertheless it’s an important one to clock. For one, it’s an example of Musk quietly downgrading his own projections, considering he said in 2020 that Tesla would sell 20 million cars annually by 2030 . And also because I think this one in particular is going to come back and bite him in the ass.
Musk’s goal to hit 5 million vehicles sold annually by 2030 would require a complete reinvention of Tesla’s business model, and not in the way he is currently trying to rewrite the company’s mission. After back-to-back delivery declines — falling from a peak of 1.81 million in 2023 to 1.64 million in 2025 — the company would need to sell a shit ton of vehicles to meet that goal. And it neither has the right vehicles nor enough factory space to do so.
Musk’s goal to hit 5 million vehicles sold annually by 2030 would require a complete reinvention of Tesla’s business model, and not in the way he is currently trying to rewrite the company’s mission
But this is Tesla we’re talking about, the company that traffics in the impossible. Could Musk pull it off? Well, that depends. Do you think the company will actually sell its flying Roadster to customers ? If so, then yes, Tesla can probably do it. After all, Elon would never lie to you, would he? But if you’re one of those people who think the Roadster was a cool demo but an absurdly unrealistic consumer product , then read on.
First, let’s take a look at Tesla’s annual delivery numbers.
Sales volume peaked in 2023, and since then has dropped for two years in a row. So far this year, Tesla has sold 1,324,681 vehicles, meaning it would need to sell 311,448 vehicles in the fourth quarter just to avoid a third straight year of declines. That seems eminently doable, especially given Tesla’s habit of offering aggressive deals toward the end of the year as a way to clear out inventory and boost those final numbers. In all likelihood, Tesla will sell enough vehicles in Q4 to give it a nice bump over its annus horribilis of 2025 . (Analysts are predicting 1.82 million for the full year, which would be the company’s best so far.)
So, to explore how Tesla can get to 5 million by 2030, we need to take into account something called compound annual growth rate, or CAGR. This is the percentage by which sales would need to grow every single year to get from where it is now to where Musk wants it to be. You calculate it by taking your target value (5 million) and dividing it by your starting value (1,636,129) to find the overall factor by which Tesla’s sales would need to grow. So the company faces a daunting 25 percent CAGR to get to Musk’s stated goal of 5 million cars sold annually by 2030.
Musk would argue this is achievable given Tesla’s current transformation from electric vehicle manufacturer to global leader in AI and robotics. A key pillar in this strategy is the Cybercab and the company’s Robotaxi fleet. If the company is able to successfully launch unsupervised Full Self-Driving in the second quarter of 2027 — which Tesla’s VP for Autonomy Ashok Elluswamy claimed during the earnings call — then demand for Tesla’s vehicles arguably would skyrocket. Moreover, VP for Vehicle Engineering Lars Moravy said that Tesla would try to deliver the first steering-wheel- and pedal-less Cybercabs to customers (likely fleet owners) before the end of the year. If Tesla can create an entirely new sales channel by selling Cybercabs to fleet owners, rather than relying solely on individual retail buyers, then perhaps 5 million cars isn’t so much of a reach.
And yet! A closer look at Tesla’s current product lineup reveals some structural deficiencies. Over 96 percent of the company’s sales depend on just two vehicles: the Model 3 and Model Y. Tesla discontinued the Model S and Model X earlier this year to make room at its plant in Fremont, California, for the production of its humanoid robot. The Cybertruck has been a sales flop, missing its initial targets by a wide margin. The Roadster may fly, but the hypercar is a nothingburger with regards to Tesla’s automotive business. (Musk himself admitted the Roadster was a “small potato” project that won’t move the needle financially.)
A closer look at Tesla’s current product lineup reveals some structural deficiencies
That leaves the Cybercab and the Semi. The latter represents a significant piece of the puzzle. As Tesla ramps up Semi production at its Nevada factory , selling large electric trucks to commercial delivery fleets could give the company a profitable way to ship tens of thousands more heavy vehicles each year, expanding its business beyond consumer cars. But it’s clear from Musk’s statements that he thinks Tesla’s best hope rests with the Cybercab.
The chips are stacked against the gilded two-seater. Before Tesla can sell or operate thousands of fully driverless cars on public roads, governments around the world have to adapt to the new technology. Getting government approval takes time and varies state by state and country by country . And Tesla is not the most persuasive company when it comes to creating new rules. Federal regulators are already scrutinizing whether the company skirted the law by rolling out the Cybercab in Austin, Texas. If regulators drag their feet, or if the technology isn’t 100 percent reliable in every city, companies won’t buy Cybercabs in bulk. Instead of selling millions of autonomous taxis to commercial fleets by 2030, Tesla would be left trying to sell traditional cars to individual buyers.
But Musk is such a true believer that he abandoned plans for a $25,000 mass-market EV (the so-called “Model 2”) in favor of going all in on the Cybercab. In doing so, he allowed the rest of the world — but especially China — to beat Tesla to the punch. Now we’re seeing Tesla’s market share in Europe and Asia being eroded by affordable models from BYD, Geely, and Xiaomi.
Also, Tesla is running headlong into a big factory problem. The company’s current factories can build only around 2.5 million to 3 million vehicles a year. To reach 5 million, Tesla would have to roughly double its factory space or build up to three new Gigafactories, which would take years and require massive spending, new supply chains, and a huge increase in battery production.
While Tesla remains a global force, reaching 5 million vehicles without a cheap electric car or regulatory-approved robotaxi network requires a rate of growth that seems utterly divorced from reality. Musk puts on a great show, but when it comes to delivering on his gigantic promises, he often leaves his audience scratching their heads.

Her horrified sister raised the alarm, and emergency services were scrambled, but Leiva was pronounced dead at the scene just before 12:30 p.m. Saturday.
The family was part of a tour group exploring the mountains some 9,000 feet above sea level when tragedy struck.
Leiva’s relatives were airlifted to Canazei, where her body was brought later following the recovery mission.
Forcella Pordoi, part of the Sella mountain group, is surrounded by dramatic rock faces which make the UNESCO-listed Dolomites such a popular tourist attraction.

articles.title_orig: 'Demeaning' and 'absurd': The backlash against a hugging grandparents consent ad
articles.title_zh: 'Demeaning' and 'absurd': The backlash against a hugging grandparents consent ad
articles.content_orig:
It's the consent campaign that's sparked heated debate across Ireland and beyond  - so why has a social media ad about getting a hug from your grandparents been pulled?
The ad, described by an Irish government minister as "demeaning to grandparents", sees a house's front door opening to reveal an elderly couple.
They hug their grandson and lean into embrace their granddaughter, who looks uncomfortable before it quickly cuts to a graphic and voiceover.
"Not everyone wants a hug. Even from the people who love them. Awkward? Maybe. Important? Absolutely."
The tone is light-hearted, and the aim is to promote the importance of consent for children - but it has apparently landed with a thud in Ireland and with many online.
The ad, one of three, is part of a campaign called We-Consent, run by the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC).
The backlash has opened up a debate about changing norms, the role of family and how best to teach consent to children.
While some have described it as a waste of money, others have defended it as showing how children have differences when it comes to boundaries and that it is "not campaigning against grandparents".
Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan has been an instrumental critic - his department is one of the sources of funding for the campaign and its removal came after his officials intervened.
He said the video "does not represent the views of the government".
"It was both inappropriate and demeaning to grandparents and has been removed by DRCC following my officials engagement with them.
"While it is vital to ensure that people understand the concept of consent when it comes to sexual relationships, this video did not advance that aim and in many ways was counterproductive."
In a statement to Irish broadcaster RTÉ, the DRCC said the videos were "premised on the idea that boundaries should be respected from an early age and to respect others' boundaries too".
"We are going to remove the videos from our social media channels while we reflect on whether they are having the positive effect we want them to have," it added.
Fine Gael Senator Gareth Scahill, who is among the critics, said the video was a waste of resources.
"What's concerning here is public money has been used to fund an ad which at best has been ill-thought out, and at worst is offensive and potentially damaging to our older population," he said, adding that this "publicly-funded social media video is a million miles off the mark".
"What's next? Will we need to sign consent forms at arrival halls in Dublin, Shannon, Knock and Cork airports this Christmas before we can greet family members?"
A spokesperson for the Department of Justice said the videos were "produced by DRCC at low cost using volunteers and are not part of a government advertising campaign".
Meanwhile, Dr Eoin O'Malley, an associate professor at Dublin City University, said he believes the advert is the latest example of the state overreaching.
"You are seeing people pushing ideas that are beyond mainstream," he said.
O'Malley said that the importance of consent is reasonable to most people, but that the video is too extreme.
"The idea that there needs to be an ad telling grandparents that they shouldn't hug their grandkids, that they should look for permission in advance of that, seems absurd to most normal people.
"The Irish constitution is very clear that the family is the primary unit for teaching children and for raising children, and so to some extent this is kind of going beyond that."
However, the campaign has its defenders too.
Academic Dr Órfhlaith Campbell said it is not an attack on grandparents but instead aimed to highlight the importance of consent.
"The ad is highlighting differences in children's needs and the imp (sic) of consent. It is not campaigning against grandparents. Dear god in heaven!!!" she wrote on X .
An account named Danny Boy said it wasn't "discouraging grandparents from hugging children" but was "encouraging children to speak up" if they feel uncomfortable.
University of Galway academic Dr Eoin Daly said that while the video was "patronising", the message was correct.
Fine Gael councillor Lorraine Hall also defended the advert, and said the message of the video was intended to be "figurative" rather than "literal".

articles.title_zh: Race to update services' computer systems after cyber-security flaw found
articles.content_orig:
Organisations and businesses are still scrambling to update their systems after cyber-security flaws were revealed in a widely-used programming language, PHP.
Websites around the world were taken offline on Wednesday and Thursday after the developers of PHP said "critical vulnerabilities" were found in the back-end language, used in web development for decades.
Researchers warned the "severe" flaws could expose millions of sites using it to potential hacks if left unpatched - and the UK government was among those to take some sites offline as a precaution.
There have been no successful attacks reported so far, but experts say any impact may take time - even months - to become fully apparent.
Downing Street said on Thursday "some" limited government services "may be offline" while security work was being carried out.
"The information I have is that 32 Government services are unavailable and four are partially unavailable," tech minister Baroness Lloyd of Effra told the House of Lords.
She attributed this to having "largely resulted from precautionary measures taken to protect systems while security updates and mitigations are applied".
The government did not specify which services were taken offline - but it said no large UK public-facing critical services had been affected.
A spokesperson said work had already taken place across government to "identify and fix potential exposures to our systems and our experts are continuing to work closely with both OpenAI and international partners on this issue".
"But this does not mean they were hacked, and work continues to resolve any issues," they added.
Olly Whitehouse, chief technology officer of the National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), called the event "unprecedented".
"It will be universally felt, I suspect," he told BBC Radio 4's World At One.
But he said there were "no indications" of any successful breaches by hackers.
He said the NCSC was "starting to see positive confirmation" that advice sent to those affected had been received and was being acted on.
Cyber-security lecturer Rory Hopcraft told the BBC the government needed to make sure that its own infrastructure was up-to-date.
"Hacking has been around for many years," he said.
"The government are the ones who set the rules for other organisations... they just need to effectively be practising what they're preaching at this point."
Dean Presley, who has a garage in Chepstow, South Wales, told BBC Your Voice he had been unable to properly process MOTs online.
He said his computer system had been down since Wednesday morning, and while he has experienced outages before, they have not lasted this long.
"MOTs can be conducted and they're legal but none of the paperwork and certificates can be printed and they're not on the system," Dean said.
He said this has forced him to write everything on paper documents, leading to delays for customers.
PHP stands for PHP: Hypertext Preprocessor.
It's a programming language which runs on a web server, behind the scenes of a website, and effectively lets you see the sites you visit.
When you go to a site, PHP is the code which collects data and effectively turns it into a page you can read.
It was developed in the early 1990s to help serve dynamic web pages and applications, but still powers lots of platforms today.
PHP has been used across a wide range of platforms including Wikipedia, online shops and WordPress – the system behind many websites - as well as to write tools to build web apps, with Laravel, Symfony and Drupal among popular PHP frameworks.
According to cyber-security firm Wiz , which helped uncover the critical PHP vulnerabilities surfaced this week, PHP powers 70% of the world's websites.
And it said the flaws - now coined "php2shell" - were inherent in the language itself, affecting many past versions of it.
The PHP Foundation, the non-profit which maintains the programming language, warned this meant that, under the right conditions, an unauthenticated attacker would be able to remotely execute code on servers running PHP.
Some large organisations said they had seen a high volume of attempts to breach their systems.
Matthew Prince, the boss of internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare, wrote on X on Thursday that the company saw "thousands" of attempts to exploit the PHP vulnerabilities across its network in the 10 hours before it was publicly announced.
"That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and millions now," he added.
Amazon also says it saw hackers attempt to exploit the flaws, but its websites were operating as normal.
While the impact of the PHP flaw remains to be seen, disruption continued for businesses and organisations after many sites were taken down on Wednesday.
The website of a Dutch agency specialising in cyber-security, Finland's government and parts of Wikipedia, taken temporarily offline, had returned to business as usual by Thursday.
But a number of sites appeared to have been taken offline on Thursday, as operators rushed to check if PHP might be running within their systems or if any patches were required.
In France, telecommunications company Orange also said it had suspended access to certain services globally while it deployed security fixes.
According to some cyber-security researchers using scans to check servers at risk of the PHP vulnerability, the rate of organisations implementing patches - but not as quickly as might be hoped globally.
"The window to respond has shrunk dramatically," said Matt Hull, VP of cyber intelligence and response at global cyber security company NCC Group.
"A few years ago, attackers might have taken weeks to exploit a vulnerability. Now, it can be days or hours."
Hull also highlighted the extent of the task facing developers and engineers working to deal with the issue.
"Several days into this incident, security professionals might already be dealing with significant burnout," he said, urging a need to "make time to rest, share the workload and look after each other".
"Resilience depends on people as much as technology."

On November 23rd, on iOS and Android, the Browse for Me and “other AI features” will be disabled and “you will no longer be able to sign in or sync your tabs.” On December 22nd, the Arc browser won’t be accessible on macOS or Windows, Arc accounts will be deactivated, and Arc Search for Android will be removed from Google Play.
The Browser Company has an FAQ about how to import your data into Dia, if you want to move to that browser. Dia is now where the company is focused, “including our whole security team.”
Arc, which had a lot of big ideas about browsers that have popped up in other browsers since. The Zen browser, which is based on Mozilla’s Gecko engine, is a frequent recommendation for people looking for an Arc-like experience. Last year, Atlassian acquired The Browser Company for $610 million .

articles.title_orig: Brazilian election: Lula seeks Bolsonaro's disqualification over alleged Meta interference
articles.title_zh: Brazilian election: Lula seeks Bolsonaro's disqualification over alleged Meta interference
articles.content_orig:
Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's campaign has requested the disqualification of right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro in the lead up to the final round of the presidential election on Sunday over alleged interference by social media company Meta.
In a petition filed to the country's top electoral court on Wednesday, the leftist incumbent president accused Meta, the tech giant behind Whatsapp, Instagram and Facebook, of limiting its content to boost Bolsonaro's campaign.
In response, Bolsonaro filed a petition seeking to disqualify Lula over what he said was the mass dissemination of government posts on WhatsApp.
The company has denied the campaigns have been treated unequally.
It comes after UN experts said on Wednesday that they were concerned about reports of discrepancies in the ability of each campaign to reach voters on Meta's platforms.
A report led by the UN's special rapporteur on freedom of expression said Meta must ensure a level playing field online during the election.
It cited incidents including "temporary interruptions of one candidate's campaign account; differences in audience engagement, user feeds, view counts and reach; restrictions on that campaign's Instagram posts".
"Information, including from Meta employees, suggests that accounts linked to one side of the presidential race were disproportionately curtailed," it read.
Meta has denied taking action to favour one side of the election and has said it would comply with an order from a Brazilian court to treat Bolsonaro and Lula equally.
Lula's campaign had previously filed a complaint alleging that accounts and content related to Bolsonaro were boosted.
Users also reported that Meta's artificial intelligence tools were not generating images related to Lula.
Brazilians will head to the polls on Sunday as Lula seeks a fourth term in office.
Bolsonaro beat Lula in the first round of voting on 4 October by a narrow margin, but fell short of the 50% of valid votes needed to win outright.
On Wednesday, Lula's campaign filed a petition to Brazil's Superior Electoral Court (TSE) for Bolsonaro and Alfredo Gaspar, his candidate for vice-president, to be investigated over "abuse of economic power and improper use of social network".
The petition also seeks to make Bolsonaro ineligible to stand for election for eight years following the 2026 election.
Meanwhile, Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of convicted former president Jair Bolsonaro, accused his rival of "abuse of political and economic power".
He claims the government has used personal data taken from official databases to send mass messages on Whatsapp to promote social programmes.
Opinion polls suggest Sunday's run-off will be extremely close, with little separating the two as Brazil's 159 million registered voters prepare to go to the ballot boxes.

articles.title_orig: Two CVSS 9.0 Linux KSMBD RCE Flaws Disclosed on Public Mailing Lists Before Kernel Fixes
articles.title_zh: Two CVSS 9.0 Linux KSMBD RCE Flaws Disclosed on Public Mailing Lists Before Kernel Fixes
articles.content_orig:
Linux servers running KSMBD, the kernel's built-in SMB server, are exposed to two publicly reported remote code execution flaws rated 9.0 by Trend Micro's Zero Day Initiative , with no fix yet in the mainline kernel.
One of them, ZDI-CAN-33774, can be triggered before any network authentication. The other, ZDI-CAN-33549, requires the SMB Direct transport and an RDMA-capable network interface.
ZDI-CAN-33549 is an integer underflow in KSMBD's SMB Direct path. A client can supply RDMA buffer descriptors in which the first is longer than the declared payload, causing the server's size counter to wrap and allowing a subsequent memory copy to overrun the end of an allocated buffer.
It requires three things: an RDMA-capable interface (hardware or the rxe software driver), a writable KSMBD share, and a client negotiating SMB Direct.
ZDI-CAN-33774 requires no authentication, exposing any server running KSMBD on port 445. The flaw is a race in how KSMBD assigns its handler table: a burst of short SMB1 packets followed by an SMB2 packet in the same TCP write causes workers to handle SMB1 data with an SMB2 handler, reading past the end of the shorter buffer. A path to writing past the buffer also exists once an attacker has access to a share.
As of Thursday, neither flaw has a named fix in the mainline kernel or in linux-next , the integration tree that feeds it. Linux news site Phoronix said SMB Direct maintainer Stefan Metzmacher submitted a fix for ZDI-CAN-33549 targeting the next kernel development cycle, but this has not been confirmed elsewhere.
Fixes to mainline typically take weeks to reach stable branches and distribution kernels after that. Neither flaw has a CVE identifier, since the kernel project assigns those only after a stable-tree fix is available.
Running systemctl status ksmbd or lsmod | grep ksmbd confirms whether the module is active. Red Hat Enterprise Linux does not include KSMBD by default, according to Red Hat's support documentation .
The ZDI reports credit TrendAI, Trend Micro's AI scanner, as the finder. The Linux kernel's security documentation , updated in May 2026 following guidance from Linus Torvalds , states that bugs found by AI tools are, by definition, already public and should be sent to subsystem developer lists.
ZDI's routing appeared to follow that logic, copying public mailing lists alongside the private kernel security address without attaching patches to any of the reports.
Stable-kernel maintainer Greg Kroah-Hartman replied to three of the five kernel reports within minutes of each other. To the report on the VMware GPU driver , he wrote: "For some reason you sent this to public lists, and did not include a patch, so there's not much we can do with this." On the NVMe driver report , seventeen seconds later: "Again, no patch, and sent to a public list? Please fix your submission process."
Three of the five kernel reports are not related to SMB. ZDI-CAN-33367 , discovered by researcher p1r0x , is a local privilege escalation in the kernel's networking stack that requires local access. ZDI-CAN-34068 is a local privilege escalation in the VMware virtual GPU driver, ZDI-CAN-34076 is an information disclosure in the NVMe target driver, and neither affects KSMBD servers.
A sixth ZDI report, ZDI-CAN-32005, is a buffer overflow in ConnMan , a network daemon separate from the Linux kernel.

French president also says he will decide on concrete ‘next steps’ for the next nationwide demonstrations

Emmanuel Macron has said “illegitimate” demonstrations will be banned over the coming days as France seeks to get a grip on civil unrest after some of its worst street violence in years erupted on the fringes of cost of living protests at the weekend.
Speaking after a ​meeting with intelligence officials and senior ministers, the French president said on Thursday that demonstrations organised by recognised groups would be allowed to go ahead, although their routes could be changed.
Protests requested by “individuals or groups with no legitimate authority” would be banned, Macron said. Requests by organisations such as trade unions would be “examined in accordance with the law” but they might have to use alternative routes.
The measures were necessary to protect city centres, businesses and public buildings, he said, adding: “The rules are simple and I think they’re commonsense. The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations in the coming days.”
Macron blamed much of last weekend’s unrest and looting on rioters who came expressly to loot, but said the worst of the violence was due to “political and seditious acts by ultra far-left groups who aimed to bring down the republic”.
“The priority is a return to calm,” he said, adding that he would chair a defence council meeting of key ministers on Friday to decide concrete “next steps” for new nationwide demonstrations called for Saturday and afterwards.
An initial police ban on a student protest planned in Paris for Thursday was overturned by a court, but marches also scheduled for the day in Grenoble, Rouen, Le Havre and Toulon were halted.

Authorities have already declared a ban on “all protests” on Saturday in the centre of Lyon, France’s third-biggest city, where between 200 and 300 shops were ransacked and looted last weekend and the tourist office was set ablaze.
Authorities in Marseille, Nice and Toulon announced similar bans for Saturday. In Paris, a march planned for Saturday to be held in the east of the capital, starting at the Place de la Bastille, was authorised but banned from heading into the city centre.
However, a separate march through the capital planned for Saturday by students and some members of the gilets jaunes (yellow vests) movement, whose protests over fuel prices rocked France in 2018 and 2019, would not be permitted, authorities in the capital said.
France’s main student union, UNEF, has also called ‌for rallies on Saturday. Businesses in central Paris and other cities had already begun boarding up their windows and hiring private security in preparation for violence, French media reported.
The justice minister, Gérald Darmanin, said 174 of the 2,500 people arrested since last weekend’s rioting had been remanded in custody and more than 900 were being prosecuted. Two people have been arrested after Limoges town hall was set on fire.
The prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, was hosting a meeting of key figures from France’s main political parties on Thursday to hear their views and seek cooperation, and was due to meet several big-city mayors later in the day.
The tough security response has included partial night-time curfews in parts of several cities including Paris, as well as bans on gatherings in areas such as around the Élysée presidential palace, the parliament and the city’s main train stations.
The demonstrations began last month in a high school in Créteil, south-east of Paris, over staff shortages and dilapidated buildings, and spread nationwide, with strikes, blockades and demonstrations by high-school pupils around the country.
Those demonstrations have morphed into larger protests over soaring living costs, six months before next year’s presidential elections, which will choose Macron’s successor.
